title: The king and the fawn
hookLine: King Bharata raises an orphaned fawn until it fills his mind, and Yoga names the groove: samskara
carry: samskara: what you repeat, you become
tomorrow: a great archer drops his bow and weeps. what does Krishna call yoga?

cards: King Bharata has given up his throne to live as a hermit by a river, praying. One morning a pregnant doe comes to drink. A lion roars.

She leaps the river in terror, her fawn is born in mid-leap and drops into the water, and she dies. Bharata pulls the tiny fawn out and raises it. He feeds it, worries when it wanders, watches the forest for it.
Slowly, his prayers fill up with the fawn. And when he dies, the Bhagavata Purana says, his last thought is the fawn. He's born again as a deer.

teach.b: But a deer who remembers. He stays near the hermitages, and in his next birth, as a brahmin's son, he guards his mind so carefully that people take him for a simpleton: Jada Bharata, Bharata the dull.
The story is a picture of a Yoga word. Samskara: the trace an experience leaves in the mind. Patanjali's word for the mind's movements is vritti, a turning.
Vyasa, the Sutras' early commentator, ties them in a wheel.
Turnings leave traces, and traces give rise to turnings again. Every thought of the fawn wore Bharata's groove a little deeper, until it was the thought he died with.

The Gita says it plainly: whatever a person remembers at the end, they go to, having been absorbed in it. That's why Hindus hope to have God's name on their lips at the end, and why many families chant it at a deathbed.
But the wheel turns both ways. Near the end of the first chapter comes the hopeful line: a trace born of true insight blocks the other traces.

teach.h: WHAT YOU REMEMBER AT THE END.
teach.b: What wore the old path can wear a new one.
That's the reason for so much repetition in Hindu practice: japa on a mala, the same prayer each morning, the same lamp each evening.
It isn't empty habit: each round lays a trace you'd be glad to be carried by. And samskara has a second home in Hindu life: the rites that mark a life, from a child's naming to a wedding.

how: Hindus practice japa, repeating a divine name, often on a mala of 108 beads, and many families chant God's name at a deathbed; teachers of the Yoga Sutras explain why steady repetition matters: each round lays down a new samskara, a trace in the mind.

o: a way to wipe every old memory out at once
a word that only ever means a wedding or naming rite
a trace in the mind that each repetition wears deeper

games.q: the wheel in Yoga — tap the pairs.
p: the groove his last thought ran in

s: Bharata was reborn as a deer for being cruel to animals
the opposite: he loved the fawn so constantly that it filled his mind at death.
Vyasa says turnings and traces feed each other in a wheel
turnings leave traces, and traces give rise to turnings again.
Patanjali says old traces can never be changed
he says a trace born of true insight blocks the other traces.

games.q: you've said one line of a mantra wrong so often that the wrong version comes out on its own. in Yoga's terms, what changes it?
o: saying it right again and again: new samskaras
games.why: repetition. each right round lays a new trace; what wore the old groove can wear a new one, which is why Hindu practice repeats.

practice: Try japa, the way it's done. Count on the joints of your fingers, or on a mala if you have one, and say a divine name slowly, eleven times: Rama, or Om namo Narayanaya, or Om.
When the mind wanders down its old path, notice, and come back on the next count. If you don't pray, repeat a word for who you want to become, and count the returns, not the wanderings.

wordCard.voice: Yoga. Vyasa's wheel: turnings leave traces, traces make turnings, and a trace of insight can wear a new path. Samskara is the trace.

orig.note: Sanskrit: in Yoga, the trace an experience leaves in the mind; elsewhere in Hindu life, a rite that marks a life.

carryVoice: Your line: samskara, what you repeat, you become. Bharata's fawn wore the groove one thought at a time. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 5.7–5.9 (Bharata, the fawn, rebirth as a deer, and Jada Bharata)
Vyasa, Yoga Bhashya on 1.5 (turnings produce traces and traces produce turnings; the wheel turns ceaselessly)
Yoga Sutras 1.50 (the trace born of truth-bearing insight obstructs other traces)
Bhagavad Gita 8.6 (whatever state one remembers at the end, to that one goes, having been absorbed in it)
